title: Query-performance concepts
objective: Write queries the engine can execute cheaply: sargable predicates, early filters, only the columns you need, pre-aggregation before joins — and know how indexes (SQLite) and pruning/clustering (Snowflake) reward those habits.
context: Snowflake bills by warehouse-seconds. The data team's monthly bill doubled after a dashboard went live, and the culprit is a handful of queries that scan everything and join before they filter. You're asked to rewrite them — with identical results.

exercises.title: Make the year filter sargable
exercises.question: Ops dashboard query: `SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025' GROUP BY order_status`. It can't use idx_orders_date. Rewrite it.
exercises.prompt: Return order_status and orders (count) for orders placed in calendar year 2025, using a range predicate on the bare order_date column (order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01').
hints: Sargable = Search ARGument ABLE: the column must appear on its own on one side of the comparison.
Use a half-open range: >= first day, < first day of the next period.
exercises.why: Half-open date ranges are correct for DATE and TIMESTAMP columns alike, and they enable index seeks in SQLite and partition pruning in Snowflake.

recall.a: It's also correct for timestamps (2025-12-31 14:00 is < 2026-01-01 but > '2025-12-31').

exercises.snowflake: SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE AND order_date < '2026-01-01'::DATE GROUP BY 1;  -- prunes partitions; YEAR(order_date) = 2025 may not

exercises.title: Index inventory
exercises.question: Before tuning, the DBA asks which tables have secondary indexes and on how many columns.
exercises.prompt: Query sqlite_master (type = 'index') and return table_name (tbl_name) and index_count (number of indexes on that table).
hints: sqlite_master is a catalog table: columns type, name, tbl_name, sql.
Filter type = 'index' and group by tbl_name.
SELECT tbl_name AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS index_count FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' GROUP BY tbl_name;
exercises.why: Knowing what physical structures exist (indexes in SQLite/Postgres, clustering keys in Snowflake) is the first step of any tuning conversation.

recall.q: Snowflake's catalog equivalent for metadata queries?
recall.a: INFORMATION_SCHEMA views (TABLES, COLUMNS, ...) and SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE; clustering via SHOW TABLES / SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT table_name, clustering_key FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'PUBLIC';

exercises.title: Filter early: December 2025 order lines
exercises.question: This query joins everything and filters at the end: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT o.*, oi.*, p.* FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id=oi.product_id) WHERE order_date LIKE '2025-12%'`. The dashboard only needs a few columns.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_date, product_name, quantity and line_total (quantity * unit_price) for order lines of orders placed in December 2025 (any status). Filter orders with a sargable date range first and select only these columns.
hints: Start from the smallest filtered set: orders in December 2025.
A range on order_date (>= '2025-12-01' AND < '2026-01-01') uses idx_orders_date; then idx_order_items_order serves the join.

WITH dec_orders AS (SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-12-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01') SELECT d.order_id, d.order_date, p.product_name, oi.quantity, oi.quantity*oi.unit_price AS line_total FROM dec_orders d JOIN ...
exercises.why: Modern optimizers often push filters down for you — but not through every construct (LIKE on a derived column, window functions, UNIONs). Writing it early is cheap insurance.

recall.q: Which two indexes can this query use?
recall.a: idx_orders_date for the date range and idx_order_items_order for the join.

exercises.snowflake: Same query; the date range prunes orders' micro-partitions, and naming 5 columns means only those columns are read.

exercises.title: Pre-aggregate before joining
exercises.question: Product revenue report: the old query joins products to every order line, then groups by product name and list price. Rewrite it to aggregate order_items first.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, units_sold and gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) for every product that has at least one line on a valid order. Aggregate the lines per product_id in a CTE before joining products. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: The aggregation only needs order_items (+ a status filter); product_name can be attached afterwards.
Join 22 aggregated rows to products instead of 134 valid order lines.

WITH product_sales AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold, SUM(quantity*unit_price) AS gross_revenue FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE ...) GROUP BY product_id) SELECT ... JOIN products ...
exercises.why: Aggregating at the fact table's key and joining dimensions last shrinks the join and avoids grouping by long text columns.

recall.q: Why group by product_id rather than product_name?
recall.a: IDs are unique and compact; names can collide and make grouping slower and ambiguous.

exercises.snowflake: Same pattern; in Snowflake large joins are hash joins whose cost grows with input size, so shrinking inputs first matters most.

exercises.title: Avoid the double fan-out: orders and returns per customer
exercises.question: A customer-health query joins customers → orders → order_items → returns and then uses COUNT(DISTINCT ...) everywhere to undo the duplication. Make it cheap and obviously correct.
exercises.prompt: For every customer (all 20), return customer_id, valid_orders (number of valid orders, order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) and returned_lines (number of returns rows on lines of that customer's orders, any status). Both are 0 when there are none. Pre-aggregate each metric in its own CTE and LEFT JOIN them to customers.
hints: Two independent one-to-many paths from customers → aggregate each separately.
Each CTE has one row per customer, so the final LEFT JOINs can't multiply rows.

WITH order_counts AS (... GROUP BY customer_id), return_counts AS (SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) ... FROM returns r JOIN order_items oi ... JOIN orders o ... GROUP BY o.customer_id) SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(oc.valid_orders,0) AS valid_orders, COALESCE(rc.returned_lines,0) AS returned_lines FROM customers c LEFT JOIN ...
exercises.why: COUNT(DISTINCT) over an exploded join works but costs a big intermediate result and a sort. Pre-aggregation is cheaper and makes the grain explicit.

recall.q: Why is COUNT(DISTINCT ...) after a fan-out join a performance smell?
recall.a: The engine first builds the multiplied rows, then de-duplicates them — work you could avoid by aggregating first.

exercises.snowflake: Identical CTEs; in the Query Profile the old version shows a join whose output rows greatly exceed its inputs ('exploding join').

exercises.title: Latest five valid orders, cheaply
exercises.question: The homepage widget shows the five most recent valid orders with their line counts. The old query counted lines for all 60 orders, then sorted and limited.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_date and line_count (number of order_items lines) for the 5 most recent valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), ordered by order_date descending then order_id descending. Pick the 5 orders first, then count their lines.
hints: Top-N first: ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5 inside a CTE (idx_orders_date can serve the sort).
Then join only those 5 orders to order_items and count.

WITH latest AS (SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE ... ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 5) SELECT l.order_id, l.order_date, COUNT(oi.order_item_id) AS line_count FROM latest l LEFT JOIN order_items oi ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ...;
exercises.why: Reducing the row set before the expensive step (join + aggregate) is the same idea as filter-early, applied to Top-N queries.

recall.q: Why repeat ORDER BY in the outer query?
recall.a: A CTE's ORDER BY doesn't guarantee the final output order; only the outermost ORDER BY does.

exercises.snowflake: Same; Snowflake's TOP-N optimisation can also skip partitions whose max(order_date) is too old to make the top 5.

worked_example.question: Which indexes exist in the practice database, and on which columns?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT m.name     AS index_name,
       m.tbl_name AS table_name,
       ii.name    AS column_name
FROM sqlite_master AS m,
     pragma_index_info(m.name) AS ii
WHERE m.type = 'index'
ORDER BY m.name;
worked_example.explanation: Four indexes: orders(customer_id), orders(order_date), order_items(order_id) and order_items(product_id) — exactly the join and date-filter columns. Primary keys are indexed implicitly. Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on your exercise answers to see them used.

recipe:
**Recipe: 5 performance habits that work on every engine**

1. **Sargable predicates** — leave the column bare: `order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'`
   instead of `strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025'`. A function wrapped around the column hides it from the
   index (SQLite) and from min/max pruning (Snowflake).
2. **Filter early** — restrict the big table before joining or aggregating (in a CTE or WHERE), not after.
3. **Select only what you need** — no `SELECT *` in production queries; columnar engines (Snowflake) read only the
   columns you name.
4. **Pre-aggregate before joining** — reduce `order_items` to one row per order/product, *then* join dimensions.
   Smaller join inputs, and no fan-out.
5. **Know your indexes / clustering** — in SQLite: `SELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index'`
   and `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN <query>` (look for `SEARCH ... USING INDEX` vs `SCAN`).

```sql
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-12-01';   -- SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_date
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2025-12';  -- SCAN orders
```
snowflake_notes:
**Snowflake has no indexes** (except on hybrid tables). Instead:

- **Micro-partitions:** every table is stored in immutable ~16 MB (compressed) columnar chunks. Snowflake keeps
  min/max metadata per column per partition.
- **Pruning:** `WHERE order_date >= '2025-12-01'` lets Snowflake skip every partition whose max(order_date) is
  earlier — often 99% of the table. `WHERE TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') = '2025-12'` or
  `WHERE DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) = ...` can defeat pruning; compare the bare column with a range.
- **Clustering:** data loaded in time order is naturally clustered by date. For big tables filtered on another
  column you can define `ALTER TABLE orders CLUSTER BY (customer_id)`; check health with
  `SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('orders', '(order_date)')`.
- **Column projection:** storage is columnar, so `SELECT *` on a 200-column table reads 200 columns. Name columns.
- **Query Profile** (Snowsight) shows *Partitions scanned vs total*, bytes spilled, and exploding joins — the
  Snowflake equivalent of `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`. `EXPLAIN USING TEXT <query>` works too.
- **Result cache:** an identical query on unchanged data returns instantly for 24 h — don't benchmark the second run.
- **Search optimization service** helps point lookups (`WHERE email = ...`) on huge tables; it costs credits.
- Pre-aggregation and early filtering matter even more: a join that explodes to billions of rows spills to disk.
common_mistakes: Wrapping a filtered column in a function (strftime, DATE_TRUNC, LOWER) — kills index use and pruning.
SELECT * in dashboards on wide columnar tables.
Joining every dimension first and grouping by long text columns instead of aggregating facts by key first.
Hiding row explosion with DISTINCT / COUNT(DISTINCT) instead of fixing the join grain.
Benchmarking Snowflake on the second run (result cache) or judging SQLite plans without EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
recall: The column appears bare (no function around it) in a comparison against a constant/range.
How does Snowflake avoid reading irrelevant data without indexes?
Micro-partition pruning using per-partition min/max metadata (helped by clustering).
SQLite command to see whether an index is used?
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN <query> — look for 'SEARCH ... USING INDEX'.
